column9: What is the main purpose of meiosis?
column14: To make two identical body cells for growth
column15: To repair damaged tissue after an injury
column16: To copy the DNA without the cell dividing
column17: To make sex cells with half the chromosomes
column28: Meiosis makes gametes (sperm and egg), the sex cells, with half the chromosome number, for sexual reproduction. Making identical body cells and repairing tissue are jobs of mitosis, and the DNA is copied in interphase before a cell divides.
column29: Meiosis happens in the reproductive organs. What kind of cell do they make?

column9: How many cells are produced from one diploid cell after meiosis is complete?
column14: One
column16: Four
column17: Eight
column28: Meiosis has two divisions. Meiosis I makes 2 cells, and Meiosis II splits each of those, for 4 haploid cells. Mitosis makes 2.
column29: There are two divisions: one cell becomes two, then each of those divides again.

column9: Human body cells have 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a human egg cell?
column28: Meiosis cuts the chromosome number in half: 46 → 23. Egg and sperm cells are haploid, so each has 23. When they join, the zygote has 46 again.
column29: Gametes have half the number found in body cells.

column9: Sex cells (sperm and eggs) are made when germ cells divide by meiosis.
column28: True. Germ cells are cells in the reproductive organs that produce gametes. They divide by meiosis to make haploid sperm or eggs.
column29: Germ cells live in the reproductive organs. What do those organs make?

column9: In human males, meiosis makes sperm cells in the ___.
column28: Sperm are made by meiosis in the testes. In females, egg cells are made by meiosis in the ovaries.
column29: Name the male reproductive organs.

column9: Your body (somatic) cells, like skin and muscle cells, are diploid.
column28: True. Body cells are diploid (2n): they have two sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent. In humans that is 46 chromosomes, or 23 pairs. Only gametes are haploid.
column29: Do body cells have one set of chromosomes or a set from each parent?

column9: A zygote is the first cell of a new organism. Is a zygote haploid or diploid, and why?
column14: Haploid, because it came from two haploid gametes
column15: Diploid, because it has a set of chromosomes from each parent
column16: Haploid, because it has only one set from the egg
column17: Diploid, because it copied the egg's chromosomes twice
column28: At fertilization, a haploid sperm (n) and a haploid egg (n) join: n + n = 2n. The zygote is diploid, with one set from mom and one set from dad.
column29: Add one set from the sperm to one set from the egg.

column9: The gametes made by meiosis are genetically identical to the parent cell.
column28: False. Gametes are haploid (half the chromosomes) and each one is genetically unique because of crossing over and independent assortment. Identical copies come from mitosis.
column29: Do brothers and sisters from the same parents look exactly alike?

column9: What are homologous chromosomes?
column14: A matching pair of chromosomes, one from each parent, with the same genes
column15: Two identical copies of one chromosome made when the DNA is replicated
column16: A pair of chromosomes that is found only in the cells of females
column17: Two different chromosomes that have fused together into one
column28: Homologous chromosomes are a pair: one from mom and one from dad. They are the same size and carry the same genes, but they can have different versions (alleles). Two identical copies from replication are sister chromatids, not homologous chromosomes.
column29: Homo- means same. You got one of each pair from each parent.

column9: Which cells in the human body are haploid?
column14: Skin and nerve cells
column16: Zygotes and embryo cells
column17: Sperm and egg cells
column28: Only gametes (sperm and eggs) are haploid, with 23 chromosomes. Skin, nerve, muscle, and bone cells are body cells (diploid, 46), and zygotes and embryo cells are diploid because they have a set from each parent.
column29: Which cells are made by meiosis?

column9: Meiosis has two rounds of division, while mitosis has only one.
column28: True. Meiosis I and Meiosis II are two divisions, which is why one cell becomes four. Mitosis is one division, making two cells.
column29: Think of Meiosis I and Meiosis II.

column9: Match each word to its meaning.
column14: Diploid (2n) :: Two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent
column16: Gamete :: A sperm or egg cell
column17: Zygote :: A fertilized egg
column18: Fertilization :: A sperm and an egg join together
column28: Diploid (2n) = two sets (46 in humans). Haploid (n) = one set (23 in humans). A gamete is a sperm or egg. Fertilization is when they join, and the zygote is the fertilized egg that forms.
column29: Di- means two. The symbol n stands for one set.

column9: Which type of reproduction depends on meiosis?
column14: Asexual reproduction, because it copies one parent
column15: Binary fission, because a bacterium splits in two
column16: Sexual reproduction, because it joins two gametes
column17: Budding, because a new organism grows off the parent
column28: Sexual reproduction joins a sperm and an egg, and those gametes are made by meiosis. Asexual reproduction, binary fission, and budding make copies of one parent without gametes.
column29: Which kind of reproduction needs a sperm and an egg?

column9: Put these steps in order to show how a new human life begins.
column14: A germ cell copies its DNA during interphase
column16: Meiosis makes haploid sperm and egg cells
column17: The zygote divides by mitosis to grow
column28: The germ cell copies its DNA, then meiosis makes haploid gametes. A sperm fertilizes an egg, forming a diploid zygote, which then grows by mitosis into a baby.
column29: Gametes must be made before they can join, and the zygote grows last.

column9: In sexual reproduction, what does each parent pass on to the offspring?
column14: A gamete carrying one set of chromosomes
column15: A body cell carrying two full sets
column16: A zygote that is already diploid
column17: A germ cell that divides by mitosis
column28: Each parent gives one haploid gamete with one set of chromosomes. The two sets combine at fertilization to make a diploid zygote.
column29: The baby gets half of its chromosomes from each parent.

column9: Which event happens during Prophase I of meiosis?
column14: Sister chromatids separate to opposite ends
column15: Two nuclei form around identical chromosome sets
column16: The cell splits into four haploid cells
column17: Homologous chromosomes pair up and cross over
column28: In Prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair up and can swap pieces of DNA (crossing over). Prophase is the first step, so nothing has been pulled apart yet: chromatids separating, new nuclei forming, and the split into four haploid cells all come later.
column29: Prophase is the 'prepare' step, before anything is pulled apart or split. Which choice fits a cell that is still getting ready?

column9: During which stage do homologous chromosome pairs line up in the middle of the cell?
column14: Metaphase II
column16: Prophase I
column17: Metaphase I
column28: In Metaphase I, the homologous chromosomes line up in pairs across the middle. In Metaphase II, chromosomes line up one by one, not in pairs.
column29: Lining up happens in metaphase. In which division are the chromosomes still in their homologous pairs?

column9: In meiosis, during which stage do the sister chromatids finally separate?
column14: Anaphase II
column16: Telophase I
column17: Prophase II
column28: In Anaphase I, the homologous pairs separate but each chromosome stays X-shaped. The sister chromatids don't separate until Anaphase II.
column29: The first division separates the pairs. Which division splits the X shapes?

column9: A species has 24 chromosomes in each body cell. Which statement is correct after Meiosis I?
column14: Each daughter cell is haploid with 24 chromosomes
column15: Each daughter cell is haploid with 12 chromosomes
column16: Each daughter cell is diploid with 24 chromosomes
column17: Each daughter cell is diploid with 12 chromosomes
column28: Meiosis I separates the homologous pairs, so each cell gets one of each pair: 24 → 12. Having one set makes the cells haploid. Meiosis II then splits the sister chromatids without changing the number.
column29: Meiosis I is the division that splits up the pairs.

column9: A fruit fly has a diploid number (2n) of 8. How many chromosomes are in each of its gametes?
column28: Gametes are haploid (n), so they get half the diploid number: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 chromosomes.
column29: 2n = 8. What is n?

column9: A dog's sperm cell has 39 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in one of the dog's skin cells?
column28: A sperm cell is haploid (n = 39). A skin cell is diploid (2n), so it has twice as many: 39 × 2 = 78.
column29: Skin cells are diploid. Gametes are haploid.

column9: Which of these make the children of two parents genetically different from each other? Select all that apply.
column14: The zygote dividing by mitosis after fertilization
column16: Each homologous pair lining up with mom's chromosome on a random side
column17: Each gamete gets an exact copy of the parent's chromosomes
column18: A random sperm joining a random egg at fertilization
column28: Crossing over mixes genes between homologous chromosomes, independent assortment (which way each pair faces is random) sends different mixes into each gamete, and fertilization randomly joins one sperm with one egg. Mitosis in the zygote makes identical copies, so it adds no new variation, and gametes are not exact copies of the parent.
column29: Look for the choices that shuffle or swap genetic information.

column9: Meiosis is a lot like shuffling a deck of cards before dealing hands. How does this explain why brothers and sisters from the same parents look different?
column14: Each gamete gets every card in the deck, so all siblings match
column15: Shuffling removes cards, like meiosis removes genes from the DNA
column16: Each gamete gets its own mix of chromosomes, like each dealt hand
column17: Each sibling gets all of the cards from only one parent's deck
column28: Shuffling (crossing over and independent assortment) means every gamete gets a different combination of chromosomes, just as every hand dealt is different. No genes are removed, and each child still gets a set from both parents.
column29: Two hands dealt from the same shuffled deck almost never match.

column9: A cat has 2n = 38. Which statement correctly compares the cells made by mitosis and by meiosis in a cat?
column14: Mitosis makes 2 cells with 19 each; meiosis makes 4 cells with 38 each
column15: Mitosis makes 4 cells with 38 each; meiosis makes 2 cells with 19 each
column16: Mitosis makes 2 cells with 38 each; meiosis makes 4 cells with 38 each
column17: Mitosis makes 2 cells with 38 each; meiosis makes 4 cells with 19 each
column28: Mitosis makes 2 identical body cells with the same number as the parent: 38. Meiosis makes 4 haploid cells with half the number: 38 ÷ 2 = 19. Cells made by meiosis never keep all 38, and mitosis never makes 4 cells or halves the number.
column29: Which process makes body cells, and which makes gametes? How many cells does each one end with?

column9: Match each process to what it does.
column14: Mitosis :: Makes identical diploid body cells
column16: Fertilization :: A sperm and egg join to form a zygote
column17: Interphase :: The cell copies its DNA before it divides
column28: Mitosis copies body cells exactly (diploid). Meiosis makes unique haploid gametes. Fertilization joins two gametes into a zygote. Interphase (S phase) copies the DNA before either kind of division.
column29: Which process is for growth and repair, and which is for making sex cells?

column9: The DNA is copied again between Meiosis I and Meiosis II.
column28: False. The DNA is copied only once, during interphase before Meiosis I. Then the cell divides twice, which is how the chromosome number ends up cut in half.
column29: If DNA were copied twice and divided twice, would the number ever get cut in half?

column9: The random way homologous pairs line up before they separate, which sends a different mix of mom's and dad's chromosomes into each gamete, is called independent ___.
column28: Independent assortment: each homologous pair lines up on its own, so which chromosomes go to which gamete is random. This is one reason every gamete is unique.
column29: Think about Metaphase I: each homologous pair lines up on its own, no matter how the other pairs line up.

column9: A human cell contains 22 autosomes (non-sex chromosomes) and one Y chromosome. What kind of cell is it?
column14: A sperm cell
column16: A body cell of a male
column17: A zygote
column28: 22 autosomes + 1 sex chromosome = 23 chromosomes, so the cell is haploid: a gamete. Only males make cells with a Y, so it is a sperm. A male body cell would have 44 autosomes + X + Y = 46.
column29: Count the chromosomes: is this cell haploid or diploid? Then ask who has a Y.

column9: A corn plant's pollen (sperm) cell has 10 chromosomes, and its egg cell has 10 chromosomes. How many chromosomes does a corn zygote have?
column28: Fertilization joins the two haploid gametes: 10 + 10 = 20 chromosomes, the diploid number for corn.
column29: The zygote gets all the chromosomes from both gametes.

column9: Why is it important that gametes are haploid?
column14: So fertilization restores the normal diploid number
column15: So gametes can divide by mitosis after fertilization
column16: So all of a parent's gametes are identical
column17: So gametes are small enough to move quickly
column28: If a 23-chromosome sperm joins a 23-chromosome egg, the zygote has 46, the normal human number. After fertilization the zygote (not the gametes) divides by mitosis, a parent's gametes are all different, and size has nothing to do with chromosome number.
column29: What happens to the number when two gametes add their chromosomes together?

column9: In which stage(s) of meiosis does the nuclear membrane break down?
column14: In Prophase I but not Prophase II
column15: In both Prophase I and Prophase II
column16: In Prophase II but not Prophase I
column17: In Telophase I and Telophase II
column28: The nuclear membrane breaks down in every prophase so the spindle fibers can reach the chromosomes. Meiosis has two prophases (I and II), so it happens in both.
column29: Each division needs the chromosomes free to move. How many divisions does meiosis have?

column9: A pea plant has 14 chromosomes in each leaf cell. How many chromosomes are in one of the sperm cells inside its pollen?
column28: Leaf cells are diploid (2n = 14). Pollen forms from cells made by meiosis, so its sperm are haploid: 14 ÷ 2 = 7.
column29: Leaf cells are body cells. Pollen carries the plant's gametes.

column9: A normal gamete gets one chromosome from each homologous pair.
column28: True. When the homologous pairs separate in meiosis, each gamete ends up with one chromosome from every pair. That is why a human gamete has 23 chromosomes, one from each of the 23 pairs.
column29: If body cells have pairs and gametes have half as many, how many of each pair does a gamete get?

column9: A germ cell has a diploid number of 2n = 18. How many homologous pairs of chromosomes does it have?
column28: Diploid cells have their chromosomes in pairs. 18 chromosomes ÷ 2 per pair = 9 homologous pairs. Its gametes will have n = 9, one from each pair.
column29: Each pair is two chromosomes.

column9: Which statement correctly describes where mitosis and meiosis happen in the human body?
column14: Mitosis happens only in the reproductive organs; meiosis happens in body cells everywhere
column15: Mitosis and meiosis both happen in every cell of the body
column16: Mitosis happens in body cells everywhere; meiosis happens only in the reproductive organs
column17: Meiosis happens in skin cells to repair cuts; mitosis makes gametes
column28: Body (somatic) cells all over divide by mitosis for growth and repair. Meiosis happens only in germ cells in the reproductive organs (testes and ovaries) to make gametes.
column29: Which process makes gametes, and where are gametes made?

column9: Put these events of meiosis in order.
column14: Homologous pairs line up across the middle
column15: Homologous chromosomes pair up and can cross over
column16: Homologous chromosomes are pulled to opposite ends
column17: Two haploid cells form
column18: Chromosomes line up one by one (not in pairs) across the middle
column19: Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite ends
column28: Prophase I (pairs form, crossing over), Metaphase I (pairs line up), Anaphase I (homologous chromosomes separate), Telophase I (two haploid cells), Metaphase II (chromosomes line up one by one), Anaphase II (sister chromatids separate).
column29: Meiosis I deals with pairs. Meiosis II deals with chromosomes that are no longer paired, and their chromatids.

column9: Which human cells have 23 chromosomes? Select all that apply.
column14: A zygote
column16: A skin cell
column17: A cell between Meiosis I and Meiosis II
column28: Gametes (sperm and egg) have 23. After Meiosis I, each cell already has 23 chromosomes, because the homologous pairs have separated. A zygote and a skin cell are diploid, with 46.
column29: For each cell, ask whether the homologous pairs have already been split up, or whether the cell came from fertilization or mitosis.

column9: A germ cell has 2n = 4. It copies its DNA and then completes Meiosis I. What is produced at the end of Meiosis I?
column14: Two cells, each with 2 chromosomes that are no longer X-shaped
column15: Two cells, each with 2 chromosomes that are still X-shaped
column16: Two cells, each with 4 chromosomes that are still X-shaped
column17: Four cells, each with 1 single chromosome
column28: Meiosis I separates the 2 homologous pairs, so it makes 2 cells with 2 chromosomes each (haploid). The sister chromatids are still joined (X-shaped) until Meiosis II.
column29: Meiosis I splits up pairs. How many pairs does a 2n = 4 cell have?

column9: A germ cell has 2n = 12. After it completes Meiosis I and Meiosis II, how many chromosomes are there in **all** of the final cells combined?
column28: Meiosis makes 4 final cells, and each one is haploid: n = 12 ÷ 2 = 6. So 4 × 6 = 24. Stopping at 6 counts only one cell, and 48 forgets that the number is cut in half.
column29: Find how many final cells meiosis makes and how many chromosomes each one gets.

column9: An organism has 2n = 4: chromosome pair A (one from mom, one from dad) and chromosome pair B (one from mom, one from dad). Counting only independent assortment, how many different combinations of chromosomes can its gametes get?
column28: Each gamete gets one A and one B. List them: A from mom + B from mom, A from mom + B from dad, A from dad + B from mom, A from dad + B from dad = 4 combinations. Crossing over makes even more.
column29: Each gamete needs one A and one B. List every way to choose mom's or dad's copy of each.

column9: Which statements are true of **both** mitosis and meiosis? Select all that apply.
column14: The DNA is copied during interphase first
column16: Spindle fibers move the chromosomes
column17: The daughter cells are haploid
column18: The nuclear membrane breaks down in prophase
column28: Both processes copy DNA in interphase, use spindle fibers, and break down the nuclear membrane in prophase. Crossing over and haploid daughter cells happen only in meiosis.
column29: Cross out anything that only happens when gametes are made.

column9: Which statements are true of meiosis but **not** mitosis? Select all that apply.
column14: Sister chromatids separate
column16: Crossing over can happen
column17: It happens in skin cells
column18: One cell ends up as four cells
column28: Only meiosis pairs up homologous chromosomes, allows crossing over, and turns one cell into four. Sister chromatids separate in both (Anaphase of mitosis and Anaphase II), and skin cells divide by mitosis.
column29: Two of the choices also happen in mitosis. Which ones?

column9: A germ cell with 2n = 10 has just finished Meiosis I. Its sister chromatids have not separated yet. How many chromatids are in **each** of the two new cells?
column28: Meiosis I separates the 5 homologous pairs, so each new cell has 5 chromosomes. Each chromosome is still X-shaped (2 chromatids): 5 × 2 = 10 chromatids. Meiosis II will split them into cells with 5 single chromosomes.
column29: First find how many chromosomes each cell has after the pairs separate. Then count 2 chromatids per X.

column9: Owen and Eli are brothers (not identical twins) with the same mom and dad, but they look quite different. Ana says, "Each brother came from a different sperm and a different egg." Ben says, "Meiosis mixed the parents' chromosomes differently in each gamete." Cal says, "Eli got more chromosomes from their mom than Owen did." Which classmates give a correct reason?
column14: Ben only
column16: Ana and Cal only
column17: Ben and Cal only
column28: Ana is right: each brother came from a different sperm and egg, and fertilization joins them at random. Ben is right: crossing over and the random way the pairs line up give every gamete a different mix. Cal is wrong: each brother got exactly 23 chromosomes from each parent, 46 in all.
column29: Check each claim on its own. How many chromosomes does every child get from each parent?

column9: A scientist finds a human cell with 23 chromosomes, and each chromosome is still X-shaped (two sister chromatids). Where is this cell in the life cycle?
column14: A body cell in G2 getting ready for mitosis
column16: A finished sperm cell ready to swim
column17: Between Meiosis I and Meiosis II
column28: 23 chromosomes means the homologous pairs have already separated (Meiosis I). X-shaped chromosomes mean the sister chromatids have not separated yet (Meiosis II). A body cell in G2 would have 46, and a finished sperm has 23 single chromosomes.
column29: Two clues: the number (23) and the shape (X). Which division has happened, and which has not?

column9: A cell in meiosis shows whole X-shaped chromosomes being pulled to opposite ends of the cell. The chromosomes going to each end are not copies of each other. Which stage is this?
column14: Anaphase II
column16: Anaphase I
column17: Telophase II
column28: Whole X-shaped chromosomes moving apart means homologous chromosomes are separating, which is Anaphase I. In Anaphase II, single chromatids (identical copies) move apart.
column29: Are the chromosomes still X-shaped? If so, the sister chromatids have not split yet.

column9: Nora uses yarn to model Meiosis I for a cell with 2n = 8. Her model ends with two cells that each have 8 single chromosomes, the same number as the parent cell. What did she most likely do wrong?
column14: She lined up the homologous pairs in the middle before splitting them
column15: She let the homologous chromosomes swap pieces before splitting them
column16: She split the sister chromatids in Meiosis I instead of the pairs
column17: She formed two new nuclei at the end of the first division
column28: Meiosis I should separate homologous pairs, giving 2 cells with 4 X-shaped chromosomes each. Splitting the sister chromatids instead keeps all 8 in each cell, like mitosis. The other three steps are correct parts of Meiosis I.
column29: Three choices describe Meiosis I correctly. Which one would keep the chromosome number the same?

column9: The gametes of an animal each have 12 chromosomes. Which describes the animal's body cells?
column14: 24 chromosomes in 12 homologous pairs
column16: 24 chromosomes in 24 homologous pairs
column17: 6 chromosomes in 3 homologous pairs
column28: Gametes are haploid (n = 12), so body cells are diploid: 2n = 24. Those 24 chromosomes form 12 homologous pairs, one chromosome of each pair from each parent.
column29: Double the gamete number for body cells. Each pair has two chromosomes.

column9: Crossing over happens between which two chromosomes?
column14: Chromosome 7 and chromosome 12 from mom
column15: The chromosome 7 from mom and the chromosome 7 from dad
column16: The two sister chromatids of the same chromosome 7
column17: Chromosome 7 and the X chromosome from dad
column28: Crossing over happens between homologous chromosomes: the matching pair, one from each parent, with the same genes in the same places. Sister chromatids are identical copies, so swapping between them would not create anything new.
column29: Crossing over happens when matching pairs line up side by side.

column9: Kai says, "If gametes were made by mitosis instead of meiosis, we could still reproduce." Test his idea. Two parents each have the normal 46 chromosomes. If their gametes, and their children's gametes, were made by mitosis, how many chromosomes would be in each body cell of their **grandchildren**?
column28: Mitosis keeps the full number, so each parent's gametes would have 46, and their children would have 46 + 46 = 92. The children's gametes would then have 92, so the grandchildren would have 92 + 92 = 184. The number would keep doubling, which is why meiosis must halve it before fertilization.
column29: Mitosis keeps the full chromosome number. Work it out one generation at a time.
